explanations.explanation: That's the hope, friend. God says, “Perhaps when the people of Judah hear about all the calamity I plan to bring upon them, each of them will turn from his wicked way.” (Jeremiah 36:3) He warns them first so they have the chance to turn. A warning is a door left open.
Egypt never comes up in this verse, friend. What God hopes for is that “…each of them will turn from his wicked way.” (Jeremiah 36:3) Packing a bag isn't the plan. Turning around is.
No hard hats needed here, friend. The verse never mentions walls. God hopes each person will “…turn from his wicked way.” (Jeremiah 36:3) That's a job for the heart, not the construction crew.

Forgive is the word, baker. God says, “Then I will forgive their iniquity and their sin.” (Jeremiah 36:3) Notice He puts the forgiveness right there beside the warning. The whole thing is built to end well if they turn.

Close, but that's not the word the verse uses. God says, “Then I will forgive their iniquity and their sin.” (Jeremiah 36:3) The promise is forgiveness for those who turn. Good news, friend, and it's right there in the text.
Nobody's keeping a ledger in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “Then I will forgive their iniquity and their sin.” (Jeremiah 36:3) Forgiving is the promise. That one's worth underlining.

Baruch it is, friend. Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, calls Baruch son of Neriah, and Baruch writes “…all the words that the LORD had spoken to Jeremiah.” (Jeremiah 36:4) One man talks and one man writes. I hope Baruch stretched his writing hand first.

Samuel doesn't show up anywhere in this chapter, friend. The writer says Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, “…called Baruch son of Neriah…” (Jeremiah 36:4) Baruch is the one holding the pen. Keep that name handy, because he's all over this story.
Joshua isn't in this scene, friend. The text says Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, “…called Baruch son of Neriah…” to write as he dictated. (Jeremiah 36:4) So Baruch gets the pen, and the job.

True, and Jeremiah is plain about it. He tells Baruch, “I am restricted; I cannot enter the house of the LORD…” and sends him there on a day of fasting to read the words “…in the hearing of the people…” (Jeremiah 36:5-6) The prophet can't go, so the scroll goes in his place. The words still get in the door.

The text says it's true, friend. Jeremiah says, “I am restricted; I cannot enter the house of the LORD…” so he tells Baruch to go and read the scroll aloud to the people. (Jeremiah 36:5-6) Jeremiah stays out, Baruch goes in, and the words still arrive.

Anger is right. Jeremiah says, “for great are the anger and fury that the LORD has pronounced against this people.” (Jeremiah 36:7) That's why this reading matters so much. He still hopes they'll bring their petition before the LORD and turn.

Good word, friend, but it's not the one in the verse. Jeremiah says, “…great are the anger and fury that the LORD has pronounced against this people.” (Jeremiah 36:7) The weight of that anger is the reason he wants them to turn. The word is anger.

Mercy is a lovely word, baker, but Jeremiah doesn't say it here. He says, “…great are the anger and fury that the LORD has pronounced against this people.” (Jeremiah 36:7) The word in the blank is anger. That's why he hopes each one will turn.

explanations.answer: The scribe's chamber in the king's palace
explanations.explanation: That's the spot. Micaiah, Gemariah's son, “…went down to the scribe’s chamber in the king’s palace, where all the officials were sitting…” (Jeremiah 36:12) He goes there right after he hears the scroll. Then he reports to them all the words he heard Baruch read. (Jeremiah 36:13)

explanations.answer: The house of Jonathan the secretary
explanations.explanation: Jonathan's house isn't in this scene, friend. The text says Micaiah “…went down to the scribe’s chamber in the king’s palace, where all the officials were sitting…” (Jeremiah 36:12) Once he gets there, he reports to them all the words he heard Baruch read. I bet Micaiah couldn't wait to tell somebody.

The guard's courtyard isn't mentioned in this scene, friend. Micaiah “…went down to the scribe’s chamber in the king’s palace, where all the officials were sitting…” (Jeremiah 36:12) That's his next stop after hearing the scroll. He walks straight into the room where the officials are.

The text says the opposite, friend. The officials send Jehudi to Baruch with the message, “Bring the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come here.” (Jeremiah 36:14) They don't tell him to stop. They want to hear it for themselves.

False is right. Nobody says stop. The officials send Jehudi with the message, “Bring the scroll that you read in the hearing of the people, and come here.” (Jeremiah 36:14) Then they ask Baruch to read it in their hearing, and he does.

explanations.answer: They turn to one another in fear
explanations.explanation: Yes. “When they had heard all these words, they turned to one another in fear…” (Jeremiah 36:16) Baruch reads, and the officials hear every word of it. Then they turn to one another, afraid. Fear is what the text reports.

explanations.answer: They laugh and wave it all off
explanations.explanation: Laughing isn't what the text reports, friend. It says that after hearing all these words, “…they turned to one another in fear…” (Jeremiah 36:16) Fear is the reaction it gives. That's not a group waving it off.

explanations.answer: They walk out before Baruch finishes
explanations.explanation: Nobody leaves early, friend. The text says “When they had heard all these words, they turned to one another in fear…” (Jeremiah 36:16) They sit through the whole reading, and then they react.

True. After the reading they say to Baruch, “Surely we must report all these words to the king.” (Jeremiah 36:16) They don't sit on it. They go to the king in the courtyard and report everything. (Jeremiah 36:20)
The text says they do, friend. The officials tell Baruch, “Surely we must report all these words to the king.” (Jeremiah 36:16) They're not keeping this one in the room. It's headed up the chain.

Hide is the word. The officials tell Baruch, “You and Jeremiah must hide yourselves and tell no one where you are.” (Jeremiah 36:19) That's the order they give the two men, friend. The text doesn't say where they hide, only that they're told to.

That's the opposite direction, friend. The officials tell Baruch, “You and Jeremiah must hide yourselves and tell no one where you are.” (Jeremiah 36:19) The officials are the ones who report everything to the king. (Jeremiah 36:20) Baruch and Jeremiah are the two told to hide.

Humble is a good word, but the officials don't say it here. They tell Baruch, “You and Jeremiah must hide yourselves and tell no one where you are.” (Jeremiah 36:19) The word is hide, friend. That's the order they give.

Jehudi, the man who carried the officials' message to Baruch, is back. “Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the scribe.” (Jeremiah 36:21) Jehudi fetches it and reads it aloud to the king. He's busy in this chapter.
Micaiah is the one who reported the words to the officials. (Jeremiah 36:13) The king is the one who sends Jehudi to fetch the scroll. (Jeremiah 36:21) That's a different job, friend.

Elishama is the scribe whose chamber holds the scroll. The text says the king sent Jehudi, who “…took it from the chamber of Elishama the scribe.” (Jeremiah 36:21) So the scroll is in Elishama's room, but Jehudi is the one sent to get it.

explanations.answer: Cuts them off and throws them in the fire
explanations.explanation: Yes, and it's hard to read. “…as soon as Jehudi had read three or four columns, Jehoiakim would cut them off with a scribe’s knife and throw them into the firepot, until the entire scroll had been consumed by the fire.” (Jeremiah 36:23) He does it again and again until nothing is left. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story.

explanations.answer: Hands them to an official to keep
explanations.explanation: Nobody's saving anything here, friend. The king cuts the columns off with a scribe's knife and throws them into the firepot. He keeps doing it “…until the entire scroll had been consumed by the fire.” (Jeremiah 36:23)

explanations.answer: Tells Jehudi to read them once more
explanations.explanation: There's no second reading, friend. After three or four columns, Jehoiakim cuts them off and throws them into the firepot. (Jeremiah 36:23) He keeps going until the whole scroll is gone.

The text says the opposite. “Yet in hearing all these words, the king and his servants did not become frightened or tear their garments.” (Jeremiah 36:24) Compare that with the officials earlier, who turned to one another in fear. (Jeremiah 36:16) This room has a very different reaction.

False is right. “Yet in hearing all these words, the king and his servants did not become frightened or tear their garments.” (Jeremiah 36:24) The officials who heard it earlier turned to one another in fear. (Jeremiah 36:16) The king and his servants don't react that way.

explanations.answer: Urge the king not to burn it
explanations.explanation: That's what they do. “…Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll…” (Jeremiah 36:25) These three speak up. The king won't listen to them.

explanations.answer: Help throw columns into the fire
explanations.explanation: These three are on the other side of that, friend. The text says they “…urged the king not to burn the scroll…” (Jeremiah 36:25) The one cutting off columns is Jehoiakim himself. (Jeremiah 36:23)

explanations.answer: Leave the room before it's done
explanations.explanation: The text never says anybody leaves. It says Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah “…urged the king not to burn the scroll…” (Jeremiah 36:25) They speak up, friend. The king still “…would not listen to them.”

True. After the officials urge him, the text says “…he would not listen to them.” and the king commands Jerahmeel, a son of the king, along with Seraiah and Shelemiah “…to seize Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet.” (Jeremiah 36:25-26) The scroll is gone and now he wants the men who wrote it. But the next verse is coming.

The text says it's true, friend. Jehoiakim “…would not listen to them.” and instead commands Jerahmeel, a son of the king, Seraiah and Shelemiah “…to seize Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet.” (Jeremiah 36:25-26) The scroll is gone and he sends men after the writers too.

The LORD. The verse says it plainly: “But the LORD had hidden them.” (Jeremiah 36:26) The king commands three men to seize Baruch and Jeremiah, and the LORD has hidden them. Remember the officials told Baruch and Jeremiah to hide back in verse 19.

Jehudi is the king's reader, friend, not their hiding place. The text says, “But the LORD had hidden them.” (Jeremiah 36:26) The king commands three men to seize Baruch and Jeremiah, and the LORD is the one who hid them.

The Rechabites don't show up in this chapter, friend. The verse says, “But the LORD had hidden them.” (Jeremiah 36:26) The king commands three men to seize Baruch and Jeremiah, and the LORD is the one who hid them.

explanations.answer: Write the very same words on another scroll
explanations.explanation: Same words, new scroll. The LORD says, “Take another scroll and rewrite on it the very words that were on the original scroll, which Jehoiakim king of Judah has burned.” (Jeremiah 36:28) A fire doesn't cancel the message. It's like a burnt batch, friend. The recipe is still good.

explanations.answer: Stop speaking to the king for good
explanations.explanation: That's not the instruction, friend. The LORD says, “Take another scroll and rewrite on it the very words that were on the original scroll, which Jehoiakim king of Judah has burned.” (Jeremiah 36:28) The words get written again.

explanations.answer: Leave Jerusalem with Baruch at once
explanations.explanation: No packing orders here, friend. The LORD says, “Take another scroll and rewrite on it the very words that were on the original scroll, which Jehoiakim king of Judah has burned.” (Jeremiah 36:28) The job is writing again.
David's. The LORD says about Jehoiakim, “He will have no one to sit on David’s throne…” (Jeremiah 36:30) That's the consequence for burning the scroll. It's a serious word.
Pharaoh isn't in this verse, friend. The LORD says about Jehoiakim, “He will have no one to sit on David’s throne…” (Jeremiah 36:30) The throne in question is David's.

That throne isn't the one in this verse, friend. The LORD says about Jehoiakim, “He will have no one to sit on David’s throne…” (Jeremiah 36:30) Verse 29 mentions the king of Babylon, but the throne here is David's.

True. The LORD says about Jehoiakim, “…his body will be thrown out and exposed to heat by day and frost by night.” (Jeremiah 36:30) I think this one is heavy, friend, and I'll leave it at that. It follows the king's choice to burn the scroll.

The text says it's true, friend. The LORD says about Jehoiakim, “…his body will be thrown out and exposed to heat by day and frost by night.” (Jeremiah 36:30) I think this is one of the heavy lines in the chapter, and we'll just let it stand.

That's the list. The LORD says, “I will punish him and his descendants and servants for their iniquity.” (Jeremiah 36:31) The consequences reach past the king himself. His descendants and servants are named right alongside him.

Baruch and Jeremiah are the two the LORD hid. (Jeremiah 36:26) The punishment names someone else: “I will punish him and his descendants and servants for their iniquity.” (Jeremiah 36:31) They aren't on that list.

The Rechabites aren't in this chapter, friend. The LORD says, “I will punish him and his descendants and servants for their iniquity.” (Jeremiah 36:31) The people named are Jehoiakim's own family and servants.

The text says there's more, friend. Baruch wrote on the new scroll “…all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.” (Jeremiah 36:32) The fire took one scroll, and the replacement came back bigger. The king didn't get the last word.

False is right. Baruch wrote down all the words from the burned scroll, and the verse adds, “And many similar words were added to them.” (Jeremiah 36:32) The king burned the first scroll, and the next one came out with more words. Like a second batch, friend, with extra sprinkles.
